accepted.label: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
accepted.description: GloVe is an unsupervised learning algorithm for generating word embeddings by factorizing a word co-occurrence matrix, capturing global statistical information.
coverage_criteria: Explain how GloVe uses a co-occurrence matrix to learn word embeddings.
Compare GloVe's approach to Word2Vec's context-window method.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone concept; represents the GloVe embedding method introduced in the self-study.

accepted.label: Implementing Feature Extraction in Python for NLP
accepted.description: Practical implementation of NLP feature extraction pipelines using Python libraries such as scikit-learn, NLTK, and spaCy, including loading text data and applying methods like CountVectorizer.
coverage_criteria: Can write code that loads text data and applies a feature extraction method (e.g., using scikit-learn's CountVectorizer).
Can describe common Python libraries used for NLP feature extraction.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone concept covering the hands-on coding aspect of feature extraction, as indicated by lesson metadata emphasizing Python.

accepted.label: Comparing Word Embedding and Feature Extraction Approaches for NLP
accepted.description: Analyzing the differences between NLP systems built using pre-trained word embeddings (e.g., Word2Vec, GloVe) versus traditional feature extraction methods, including trade-offs in dimensionality, semantic capture, and model complexity.
coverage_criteria: Can identify differences in input representation between embedding-based and feature extraction-based NLP models.
Can discuss trade-offs (e.g., dimensionality, semantic capture) between the two approaches.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone concept directly supported by the lesson description about comparing systems using embedding models and feature extraction models.

accepted.label: Building a Python Web API to Serve NLP Models
accepted.description: Developing a Python-based web API to serve NLP models, using frameworks like Flask or FastAPI, including steps to wrap a model into a REST endpoint and considerations like latency and data serialization.
coverage_criteria: Can outline steps to wrap an NLP model into a simple REST API using Python.
Can identify challenges in serving NLP models via APIs (e.g., latency, data serialization).
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone concept aligning with the lesson objective of familiarization with Python API development.

accepted.label: Creating a Basic Flask API Endpoint
accepted.description: Setting up a minimal Flask application by importing Flask, creating an instance, defining a route with @app.route to bind a view function that returns data (e.g., JSON), and running the app. This forms the basis for a simple API endpoint.
coverage_criteria: Can write a minimal Flask app that defines a route returning a string or JSON.
Can explain how the @app.route decorator registers a URL endpoint.
accepted.merge_rationale: These two candidates together teach the core pattern of creating a Flask app and defining a route, which is the foundation for building a simple API. Merging avoids fragmentation of the basic Flask API creation step.

accepted.label: Handling Dynamic URL Parameters and URL Generation in Flask
accepted.description: Using Flask's variable rules to capture dynamic parts of a URL (e.g., <int:user_id>) and employing url_for() to generate URLs for view functions, promoting maintainable and flexible endpoint design.
coverage_criteria: Can write a route with a dynamic path segment and enforce type with converters.
Can use url_for() to generate a URL to a given view function, including passing arguments.
accepted.merge_rationale: Dynamic URL variables and URL building are closely related patterns for managing dynamic endpoints and internal URL references; combining them creates a cohesive concept on handling flexible routing in Flask APIs.
